prompt.context: Nutracorp is a $5B nutrition foods company based in France. They have a broad EU presence and have excellent market share in France, Germany, and Spain. They have two lines of products: (1) Premium Infant Products — milk and solid foods for infants up to 2 years old, sold through the retail channel; and (2) Medical Nutrition Supplements — for sick patients (HIV, Cancer, Diabetes), basically a pill or powder that helps the patient recover their strength, sold through the Direct Sales Channel. The CEO feels that the growth potential for this company has maxed out in Europe.
prompt.question: The CEO would like to explore the US market. What are the key areas you would explore to determine whether this is a good idea?

clarifying_info.q: What is the prevalence of diabetes in the US population?
What is the compliance rate for diabetic patients taking supplements?
What are the sales rep salaries?
clarifying_info.a: $100K per year salary plus $100K in benefits

clarifying_info.q: What is the price of a cancer supplement dose?

exhibits.title: US Retail Channel Comparison — Infant Nutrition
exhibits.shows: A table comparing three US retail channels (Mass Retailers, Specialty Shops, Mom and Pops) across three dimensions: number of stores, total revenue, and percentage of the infant nutrition market

framework: Internal capabilities: Does Nutracorp have the operational capability to enter the US? (manufacturing, supply chain, regulatory approvals)
Channel and supplier relationships: Does Nutracorp have existing or accessible relationships with US retail and direct sales channels?
Customer overlap: Are US customers (infants, HIV/cancer/diabetes patients) comparable to EU customers in needs and willingness to pay?
Profitability: What are expected margins and payback period for US entry?
Market size and growth: What is the size and growth rate of the US infant nutrition and medical supplement markets?
Competitive landscape: Who are the incumbent US competitors and how strong are their positions?
Regulatory environment: What FDA and labeling requirements apply to infant products and medical supplements in the US?

questions.prompt: How would you go about sizing the US medical nutritional supplement market for diabetic patients? Patients take 2 supplements per day at $1.50 per supplement. Estimate the market size.
questions.guidance: Candidate should structure the market sizing as: US population × prevalence rate × compliance rate × daily consumption × price × days per year. Should ask for prevalence and compliance rates if not given. A strong answer calls out assumptions explicitly and sanity-checks the result.

math.setup: US population × diabetes prevalence × compliance rate × doses per day × price per dose × days per year

questions.prompt: How could Nutracorp grow the diabetic supplement market?
questions.guidance: A strong answer identifies multiple levers: (1) raising compliance rate among existing diabetics; (2) increase in diabetes prevalence (demographic trends, obesity); (3) increasing dosage frequency or price; (4) expanding the definition of the addressable patient set. Note that compliance has limited upside since it is already at 90%.

questions.prompt: How would US competitors react to Nutracorp entering the diabetic supplement market?
questions.guidance: Strong answer categorizes competitive responses: (1) sales force expansion to lock in relationships with doctors/hospitals; (2) product differentiation and repositioning to emphasize superiority; (3) channel blocking — exclusive contracts with distributors or hospitals; (4) increased advertising spend; (5) price cuts or bundling deals. Candidate should note first-mover advantages incumbents hold.

questions.prompt: Which US retail channel makes the most sense for Nutracorp to pursue first as it enters the infant nutrition market? (This is not a quantitative question.)
questions.guidance: A good answer asks two questions: (1) Which channel gives the best access per client? Mass Retailers: 10 chains → $10.5B market, making them the highest-efficiency channel by revenue per relationship. (2) Are there barriers to accessing the preferred channel? Mass retailers may charge premiums for shelf space; they may carry only a limited number of well-known brands, making access nearly impossible for new entrants. Specialty Retailers carry more brands and may be a more realistic entry point to build reputation before approaching mass retail. Note the data inconsistency: both Mass Retailers and Specialty Shops are listed at 40% of the infant nutrition market, yet their revenue figures differ dramatically ($10.5B vs $2.1B) — a sharp candidate should flag this. A complete answer weighs channel access economics against entry barriers.

questions.prompt: How many cancer patients would Nutracorp need to attract to break even on its medical nutrition sales force? Assume: 50 sales reps, $10M PR budget, direct costs = 80% of revenue, patients take 2 doses per day for 5 months per year, dose price = $1.
questions.guidance: Candidate should set up a breakeven: total fixed costs = revenue contribution per patient, then solve for number of patients. Watch for correct treatment of the 80% direct cost (margin = 20%). Should ask for sales rep compensation if not given.

math.setup: Fixed costs = (Sales rep cost) + (PR budget). Revenue per patient = price × doses/day × days active. Contribution margin = 20% (since direct costs = 80%). Breakeven: fixed costs = contribution per patient × number of patients
steps: Sales rep cost: 50 reps × ($100K salary + $100K benefits) = 50 × $200K = $10M
Revenue per patient per year: 2 doses/day × (5 months × 30 days/month) × $1/dose = 2 × 150 × $1 = $300

recommendation: Nutracorp should pursue US market entry, prioritizing the medical nutrition supplement segment (diabetic and cancer) given the large addressable market (~$14.8B for diabetics alone) and the existing direct sales model that transfers well to the US healthcare channel
For infant nutrition, enter via specialty retailers first to build brand recognition before attempting to negotiate shelf space with mass retailers, which will require a proven US track record
risks: Mass retailers may block access to shelf space for an unknown European brand, delaying infant nutrition revenue
Regulatory approval from the FDA for medical nutrition claims may be slower or more stringent than EU processes
US incumbent competitors (e.g., Abbott, Nestlé) have entrenched sales force relationships with hospitals and physicians that will be expensive to displace
Break-even analysis shows ~330K cancer patients needed — market feasibility depends on actual US cancer patient population and realistic market share capture
next_steps: Conduct detailed regulatory assessment for FDA approval timelines for both product lines
Map existing US competitor positions and identify white-space in the specialty retail and hospital direct-sales channels
Pilot entry with one product line in one US region to test channel economics before full rollout
Revisit the channel data inconsistency (both Mass and Specialty at 40% of market but very different revenues) before finalizing channel strategy
